title: Big US Bank Stocks Head for Longest Weekly Losing Streak Since 2008
excerpt: The KBW Bank Index is on course for a sixth straight weekly fall, down about 13% from its August record, after mixed third-quarter earnings, hot inflation data and AI disruption fears failed to lift the sector.
body:
• The 24-member KBW Bank Index fell about 1.3% this week, putting it on course for a sixth consecutive weekly loss — its longest such run since 2008.
  • The index remains in correction territory, down roughly 13% from its August record, despite third-quarter results from the largest lenders.
  • Analysts cite higher-for-longer rate risk, loan-loss worries, weak fixed-income trading in the quarter, and AI threats to banks' low-cost deposit base.
  • The index has underperformed the S&P 500 in 18 of the 21 sessions since the Federal Reserve's September 16 rate increase, a stretch Barclays says has no parallel since the index began in 1992.

Shares of the largest US banks are headed for their longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis, after a round of mixed quarterly earnings did nothing to reverse months of selling in the sector, Bloomberg News reported, via The Economic Times.

The streak

The KBW Bank Index, which tracks 24 leading lenders, fell about 1.3% this week and stayed in correction territory, down roughly 13% from its August record. The sector has seen steeper selloffs — including a drop of nearly 17% earlier this year — but six straight weekly declines would be the longest run of weekly losses since 2008. The pattern was already visible before earnings: Barron's noted last week that the index had fallen five weeks in a row, its longest streak since 2022 at that point, and was trading more than 12% below its all-time closing high set less than two months earlier.

Why earnings did not help

Third-quarter results were supposed to be the catalyst. Instead, disappointing fixed-income trading offset strength in equities, and the numbers landed alongside a hotter-than-expected inflation reading that deepened uncertainty about how aggressively the Federal Reserve will move against persistent price pressures. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan pointed to rates staying elevated for longer — a path that can slow growth and lift loan losses — and to rising funding costs for AI companies, which cloud the durability of capital-markets revenue tied to infrastructure investment.

The AI question

The longer question hanging over the sector is artificial intelligence itself. Bank stocks had already been under pressure over how AI could disrupt financial services, and Chan added that agentic AI poses a longer-term threat to the stable, low-cost deposits that underpin bank profitability. That combination — a rate path that hurts borrowers, trading revenue that disappoints, and a technology story that questions the deposit franchise — is why the selling has been persistent rather than sharp.

What to watch

Barclays analyst Jason Goldberg calculated that the KBW index underperformed the S&P 500 in 18 of the 21 trading sessions following the Fed's September 16 rate increase, with no comparable 21-session stretch since the index was created in May 1992. Because lenders transmit credit to the wider economy, a bank index that keeps sliding is read as a signal about growth, not only about bank profits. The next test is whether guidance on loan losses and deposit costs stabilizes before the streak reaches a seventh week.
